Today through Thursday: An offshore low spirals south along the 
coast, with shortwave disturbances pivoting around it being tossed
across the Inland NW. Models have nuanced differences, which will
affect some of the finer details but overall waves of rain come 
across the region over the next 48 hours with those disturbances.
The first round is forecast to increase through through this 
morning, entering southeast WA/lower ID early and tracking north 
and through the morning. By afternoon the focus for steadier 
precipitation will be over northeast WA and north and central ID. 
More isolated to scattered shower chances linger behind it and 
toward the central WA into the Cascades. Another shortwave swings 
in later this afternoon into tonight, renewing the precipitation 
potential across the region this evening into Thursday morning. 
That next round looks bit more scattered in nature.

Within all this there will also be some t-storm chances. Chances 
will be found this morning across southeast WA through the 
central/southern Panhandle. This possible thunderstorm risk this 
morning includes the Spokane/CdA area and Palouse. The incoming 
wave will encounter some unstable lapses and elevated instability,
with MUCAPE values 500 to 1000 J/kg per some guidance. The threat
area may extend a bit further west and north, per the ECMWF 
lightning flash density rates; so this will be monitored. By this 
afternoon the threat shifts largely to the mountain and southeast 
WA/lower ID. The threat wanes tonight into early Thursday, then 
picks up again Thursday afternoon toward the Cascades through 
north-central WA and the far southeast CWA. Lightning, gusty 
outflow winds and brief heavy downpours will be possible impacts.

As for precipitation amounts, models have been somewhat 
inconsistent over the past few days, vacillating between higher 
amounts and more limited amounts. The area that is looking to see 
the most limited precipitation will be central WA, where average 
rain amounts are between 0.02 to 0.15 inches. Higher amounts are 
forecast around the Cascades, between 0.15 to 0.30 inches and 
locally higher in the mountains. The eastern third of WA and ID 
have the higher rain amounts over this 48 hour period, between 
0.20 to 0.75 inches and toward 1 to 1.25 inches over the central 
Panhandle through the Camas Prairie. We will have to keep an eye 
on burn scars for potential flooding and localized urban flooding,
but it is a low confidence risk at this point. 

Winds will be breezy through the period, with the strongest winds
today out of the south to southwest gusting between 20 to 40 mph.
The strongest winds are forecast over central WA. With central WA
having less rain than other areas we will have to watch for some 
patchy blowing dust and elevated fire weather conditions, with 
winds potentially causing spread on new or existing wildfires. A 
limiting factor in this latter risk will be the higher humidity 
values. Breezy conditions are forecast Thursday as well, with 
gusts around 15-30 mph. Temperatures will be notably cooler, with 
highs in the mid-60s to upper 70s today and 60s to low 70s 
Thursday. Overnight lows will start to drop in the 30s and 40s in
spots. We will have to keep an eye toward possible frost in some 
areas over eastern WA and ID, in the sheltered valley and outlying
areas, Thursday night into Friday AM. 

Friday to Tuesday: The Inland NW remains dominated by the trough 
of low pressure. Ensembles still retrograde it off the Pacific 
coast into the early weekend, before swinging it back inland 
later Sunday into Monday. This will allow for the showery pattern
to continue, with occasional embedded t-storm chances. Models are
not entirely consistent on that detail but at this time late 
Sunday or Monday has some higher potential as the trough moves in.
Expect moderating temperatures into the weekend, though patchy 
frost may still be possible in sheltered valleys and outlying 
areas Saturday morning. /Solveig
